newsitem.title: JAPAN: E.Asia Grain - Japan, S.Korea eye Q4 corn deals.
newsitem.headline: E.Asia Grain - Japan, S.Korea eye Q4 corn deals.

text.p: Japanese and South Korean buyers are ready to buy U.S. corn, if corn premiums or freight rates fall further, traders said on Monday.
Japanese traders said they would wait for premiums to ease to below 95 U.S. cents before starting purchasing for fourth quarter supplies.
"The situation is almost the same," one Japanese corn trader said. "We're watching the freight rate. If the freight falls further, some people will launch their buying of U.S. corn."
Corn premiums are currently at about 96 U.S. cents a bushel over CBOT September futures, they said.
South Korean buyers are expected to buy U.S. corn, after a long absence from the grain market, traders in Seoul said.
Recent corn prices were now believed to be weak enough to induce South Korean buyers to cover their needs for fourth quarter shipments, they said.
"We expect some buyers will start buying corn this week for October shipment onwards," one trader said.
He said these purchases would encourage other hesitant South Korean buyers to cover their fourth quarter supplies.
Two major South Korean buying groups, the Big Feed Mills and the Korea Feed Association, are expected to buy 50,000 tonnes of corn each for October delivery onwards.
But another buying group, the National Livestock Cooperatives Federation, is expected to stay sidelined for the time being as it appears to have covered well ahead of other groups, they said.
Local flour milling companies are likely to be out of the wheat market for the time being following brisk purchases for August/September shipments last week.
Taiwan corn traders said they would remain sidelined this week, as most of the corn buying groups have covered their needs until September, Taipei traders said.

Japan's Zen-Noh, or the National Federation of Agricultural Co-operative Associations, said on Monday that it will cut the average price of feed for the third quarter of calendar year 1997 by about 200 yen a tonne.
The cuts are due to a weakening U.S. corn prices since earlier this year and lower U.S. Gulf-Japan freight costs.
But it also said feed prices for soymeal and fishmeal will rise later this year. Zen-Noh is the largest feed maker in Japan, and other feed companies are expected to follow the move.
